summary.text: Time dilation is the difference in elapsed time measured by two clocks, caused by their relative velocity or by a difference in gravitational potential.
In special relativity, an observer measures a clock moving relative to them to tick more slowly than a clock at rest in their own frame.
At everyday speeds the difference is minuscule, yet it is a practical concern for satellite navigation systems such as GPS and Galileo.

facts.label: Astronaut aging
facts.value: About 5 milliseconds less after 6 months on the ISS

facts.label: Twin result
facts.value: The traveling twin ends up younger than the one on Earth

facts.label: Near light speed
facts.value: Time slows to a stop as a clock approaches light speed

facts.label: Cosmonauts' result
facts.value: Krikalev and Avdeev each experienced about 20 milliseconds

items.prompt: Two spaceships pass each other at high speed. The crew of ship A measures ship B's clock and finds it ticking slowly. What does ship B's crew measure about A's clock?

options.label: A's clock ticks faster than their own
A's clock ticks slower than their own
A's clock ticks at exactly their rate
A's clock has stopped completely

items.explain: Each observer measures the other's clock as running slower, because each is in motion relative to the other.

items.prompt: One twin stays home while the other flies a long round trip at very high speed. When they meet again, how do their ages compare?

options.label: They are the same age, since each saw the other slow
The twin who stayed home is the younger one
The twin who flew is the younger one
The ages cannot be compared at all

items.explain: Although the effect looks symmetric, at the end of the round trip the traveling twin is younger than the sibling on Earth.

items.prompt: You watch a fast spaceship's clock through a telescope and see it ticking oddly. Why can you not use this to observe time dilation directly?

options.label: Light takes time to reach you, which muddles the readings
Telescopes always make moving clocks look slow
Time dilation only shows up in broken clocks
Moving clocks cannot be seen from a distance

items.explain: Time dilation compares clock readings, and visual readings are delayed by light's travel, so there is no direct way to see it.

items.prompt: In a thought experiment, a clock ticks once each time a light pulse completes its trip. Why does that clock tick slower when it moves sideways past you?

options.label: The clock's parts drift closer together as it moves
The light slows down to match the moving clock
The moving clock loses energy while travelling
The pulse follows a longer angled path at the same light speed

items.explain: With light's speed fixed for everyone, the longer path means a longer time between ticks from the observer's view.

items.prompt: You drive on a highway for hours and your watch seems to agree with the clock at home. Why do you not notice any time dilation?

options.label: Watches are built to cancel the effect
Everyday speeds are far too small to make a visible difference
The effect only works while standing still
Cars carry fields that shield their clocks

items.explain: Speeds reachable with current technology produce only minuscule differences, such as a few milliseconds for astronauts after months in orbit.

items.prompt: Two hikers far apart on a plain each look at the other and think the other looks tiny. How does this relate to two moving observers each seeing the other's clock slow?

options.label: Neither case is real, so both are optical tricks
Only one of the observers can be right
Each case is a symmetric effect of the viewpoint, not a contradiction
The hikers are really smaller than they seem

items.explain: Like perspective, the effect appears the same from both sides, so there is no contradiction.
